On this reading the empty sarcophagus was not the result of a robbery concealed from the king but of a reburial ordered by him.

[lehner-1997.md] Great Pyramid of Khufu: base 230.33 m, original height 146.59 m, slope 51° 50' 40". Volume about 2.6 million cubic metres; roughly 2.3 million blocks. The King's Chamber, lined and roofed in granite, measures about 10.47 m by 5.23 m and is 5.84 m high; above it are five relieving chambers roofed with granite beams, the topmost gabled. The Queen's Chamber lies on the pyramid's central axis and has a corbelled niche in its east wall. The Grand Gallery is 47 m long and 8.6 m high. The chamber floors lie at roughly 43 m (King's) and 21 m (Queen's) above the base.

[reisner-1927-hetepheres.md] Reisner reports the discovery in 1925 of a 30 m shaft (G7000x) east of the Great Pyramid containing the gilded furniture, inlaid boxes, canopic chest with preserved organs in natron solution, and the alabaster sarcophagus of Queen Hetepheres I, wife of Snefru and mother of Khufu. The sarcophagus was sealed and intact but, when opened, empty. Seal impressions in the deposit carry Khufu's name. Reisner proposed that her original tomb at Dahshur had been robbed and the body lost, and that officials reburied the surviving equipment at Giza without informing the king.

[edgar-1910.md] The Grotto is a natural cavity or fissure in the rock uncovered when the builders levelled the site; the well shaft passes through it, and the builders walled it with small courses of stone and packed it with sand and gravel as foundation fill. Investigators after Al Mamoun's time broke through the lower courses of its south wall, found only sand and gravel, and threw their spoil down the well, blocking its lower end. Wedged at the east edge of the deep hollow in the Grotto's floor lies a large granite stone of broken appearance, apparently a fragment of a larger block, with two worked surfaces at right angles to each other and parts of two large holes drilled through it.

[scanpyramids-2017.md] Three independent muon detection techniques (nuclear emulsion films placed in the Queen's Chamber, scintillator hodoscopes in the Queen's Chamber, and gas detectors outside the pyramid) detected a large void above the Grand Gallery. The void is at least 30 m long, with a cross-section similar to that of the Grand Gallery (about 8 m high), located between 50 and 70 m above ground. Its muon signal is comparable to that of the Grand Gallery, consistent with an empty (air-filled) space. Muon imaging records only material above the detector positions; the bedrock beneath the pyramid is outside the method's view from these positions. A later campaign (2023) confirmed the void and imaged a 9 m corridor behind the north face chevrons.

[reference-observable-reality.md] Unsupported objects denser than air fall; stone, metal, wood and people do not float in air. Water flows downhill and finds its own level; it does not rise in an open channel without being pushed or pumped. Nothing lifts itself: raising a mass takes work from outside it. Heat flows from hot to cold; a cool room does not warm a hot one. Sound needs air or a solid to travel and gets quieter with distance; a sound that cannot be heard outside a wall was not heard outside the wall. Fire needs fuel, heat and air. Limestone and gypsum dissolve slowly in water; dry stone stays dry when kept from water. A sealed container does not lose its contents. The sun rises in the east and sets in the west; shadows point away from the sun and are longest near sunrise and sunset. A human cannot lift a tonne, breathe under water, or live without water for weeks. Light does not bend around corners in open air. A thing cannot be in two places at once. A machine with no moving parts does no mechanical work. A building that has stood for thousands of years was not built to collapse. Nothing on Earth, left to itself, moves faster than it was thrown, dropped, or driven.

[scanpyramids-2017.md] Three independent muon detection techniques (nuclear emulsion films placed in the Queen's Chamber, scintillator hodoscopes in the Queen's Chamber, and gas detectors outside the pyramid) detected a large void above the Grand Gallery. [edgar-1910.md] The Grotto is a natural cavity or fissure in the rock uncovered when the builders levelled the site; the well shaft passes through it, and the builders walled it with small courses of stone and packed it with sand and gravel as foundation fill. Investigators after Al Mamoun's time broke through the lower courses of its south wall, found only sand and gravel, and threw their spoil down the well, blocking its lower end.
